awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Contorted Polyamide Desalination Membranes
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project investigates the commercial potential of contorted polyamide membranes for desalination. This membrane technology addresses the growing problem of water scarcity by making seawater and brackish water desalination more affordable and accessible as an alternative water supply. Contorted membranes are designed to allow water to pass through more quickly than conventional membranes while still effectively removing salt and other impurities. These membranes can be integrated into standard reverse osmosis systems, making them compatible with both new and existing desalination plants. Their higher water permeability reduces the quantity of membranes required for desalination, lowering the capital and operating costs of desalination facilities. By lowering these economic barriers to desalination, contorted membrane technology can help communities and industries secure reliable sources of clean water, advancing public health and economic development across the U.S.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of contorted polyamide membranes, a novel class of high-performance desalination materials engineered to enhance water transport and salt rejection. These membranes are synthesized using shape-persistent Tröger’s base diamine and triptycene diamine monomers, which increase the internal free volume within the polyamide network. This structural innovation yields an eightfold increase in water permeance compared to conventional polyamide membranes fabricated with m-phenylene diamine, while maintaining sodium chloride rejection greater than 99%. The enhanced permeability-selectivity of contorted polyamide membranes approaches the upper bound reported for polyamide membrane materials. These performance improvements can intensify membrane desalination processes by reducing the membrane area required for water production and lowering system-level energy demands. The membranes are designed for integration into standard spiral-wound reverse osmosis modules, ensuring compatibility with both new and existing desalination infrastructure.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF I-Corps project evaluated the commercial potential of a new class of high-performance reverse osmosis membranes developed at the University of Houston. These membranes incorporate novel contorted polyamide materials designed to increase water permeability while maintaining high salt rejection. The technology has the potential to improve the efficiency of water treatment and desalination by increasing water production within existing membrane system footprints or by reducing the energy required for water purification. The project sought to identify potential markets, understand customer needs, test these potential benefits with customers, and develop a strategy for commercializing the technology.

Through the NSF National I-Corps program, the team conducted over 100 customer discovery interviews with membrane manufacturers, water treatment equipment suppliers, consulting engineers, municipal and industrial water users, and other water industry stakeholders. These interviews provided insights into market needs, purchasing decisions, and barriers to adopting new membrane technologies. Customer discovery revealed that municipal and seawater desalination markets present substantial barriers to entry, including lengthy project development cycles, cautious adoption of new technologies, and extensive performance validation requirements. These findings led the team to shift its commercialization focus toward industrial water treatment applications, where increased water production and application-specific membrane performance may offer greater commercial value.

An important outcome of the project was the development of specific membrane performance testing protocols needed to evaluate commercial opportunities in targeted industrial water treatment markets. Customer discovery helped define relevant operating conditions, performance requirements, and validation criteria for future laboratory testing, including membrane fouling resistance under realistic operating conditions. The team also identified manufacturing scale-up and pilot-scale demonstration as critical steps toward commercialization.

The project strengthened the team's entrepreneurship and commercialization skills and expanded its network of potential customers, industry partners, and collaborators. Continued research, application-specific performance validation, and industry partnerships will help determine the potential for contorted polyamide membranes to improve the efficiency and sustainability of industrial water treatment and desalination.
